newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan struggles to snap out of real estate blues.
newsitem.headline: Japan struggles to snap out of real estate blues.

text.p: Mitsuro Shimizu has had the blues since hearing his neighbour has put her apartment up for sale.
Not because he is sorry to see her go, but because the price she is asking for her apartment in central Tokyo, 20 million yen ($180,000), is only a third of what he paid for his home in 1991.
"I was shocked by such a low price and the reality that in spite of that, she has still not found a buyer yet," said Shimizu, 49, an editor at a publishing firm.
Despite a five-year tailspin in Japan's real estate market, there are no signs that land prices have bottomed out.

Big investors such as life insurers and real estate developers, aggressive buyers of commercial land in the late 1980s, carry huge problem assets left from the collapse of the "bubble economy", making it hard for them to allocate new money for land.
Banks and non-bank financial institutions have also been reeling from property-related bad loans, a factor blocking a smooth supply of funds to the real estate market and strong economic recovery.
An advisory council to Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto unveiled a draft proposal on Wednesday to increase the liquidity of the real estate market.
It focuses on relaxing rules in big cities that limit the amount of floor space of a building on a given land area. It also urges reform of land taxes, including fixed-asset and transaction taxes.
The council, made up of leading figures from the private sector and academics, will finalise the proposal after listening to the opinions of bureaucrats.
A leading business daily, the Nihon Keizai Shimbun, said bureaucrats basically opposed the draft plan because they argued that some regulation was needed.

Hashimoto asked another advisory body in April to review the nation's basic land policy to cope with structural changes. Those changes include falling land prices, a rapid rise in the proportion of old people and the outflow of population from Japan's biggest metropolitan area centred on Tokyo.

A National Land Agency official said it was the first time in five years that Japan had reviewed its basic land policy. The advisory body will make a proposal by December, though any action may hinge on the outcome of general elections set for October 20.
"The land policy Japan adopted in 1991 was aimed at curbing soaring land prices," the official said.

"But the new policy the advisory body is discussing now is aimed at promoting effective use of land from a long-term viewpoint. We think this is needed to reactivate real estate transactions based on real demand," he said.
But he said it would be difficult to develop a proposal because panel members had different views.
Few members say land prices should fall much further below current levels, but not all agree that action should be taken to halt the decline, he said.
Japanese land prices soared in the latter half of the 1980s amid a bubble that resulted from low interest rates and banks' aggressive lending to real estate firms.
Now, after a five-year slump, land prices in big cities have fallen to the percentage of gross domestic product they held in the early 1980s.

Taking 1983 as a base of 100, nominal gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996 is 170, residential land prices in the Tokyo metropolitan areas are 161 and commercial real estate prices 157. In 1991, when land prices peaked, the percentage of nominal GDP was 160 but residential land prices in Tokyo stood at 253 and commercial land prices at 341.

"Land prices have fallen to appropriate levels from the viewpoint of historical trends, but demand for land, particularly commercial land, remains slack," said Osamu Senda, general manager at the Industrial Bank of Japan's area development and research division.
"I hope the new land policy will stimulate market sentiment."
